publish.definition: Publishing turns the saved version of an agent into the live version, so people can reach it through the channels or places you choose.
publish.analogy: Think of it like printing a final copy of a document: edits to your draft do not reach readers until you print again.

blocks.label: Draft
blocks.plain: The version you are building and testing. It can keep changing.

blocks.label: Live version
blocks.plain: The published copy that people actually use.

blocks.label: Channel
blocks.plain: A place where people reach the agent, such as Teams or a website.

blocks.label: Access
blocks.plain: Rules about who can use the agent and which channels are allowed.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: You finish the changes you want and save the agent.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The product checks that the agent is ready, and organization rules can block some channels.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The saved version becomes the live version for the channels you picked.

flow.label: Reach
flow.plain: People use the agent where they work, if they have access.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: Later changes stay in draft until you publish again.

example.input: Contoso's help desk team finishes an HR agent and wants employees to chat with it in Teams.
example.output: After publishing and connecting the channel, employees who have access can chat with the live version. New edits wait until the next publish.

whenToUse: You tested the agent and want real users to try it.
You changed the agent and need people to see the update.
You want to reach people in a new channel.
whenNot: The agent is unfinished or untested. Try it in the test chat first.
You only want to try it yourself. The test chat is enough.
publish.dataNote: When you add an agent to Teams, some agent content and chat content is shared with Teams. That data might flow outside your organization's compliance and regional boundaries.
publish.needToKnow: Publishing is what separates a draft from the version people use. Changes you make later stay in draft until you publish again. Where people can reach the agent depends on the channels you connect, the sign-in rules, and your organization's policies.
publish.demo: Show a published agent answering in a chat. Then change a small piece of wording and show that the live version stays the same until the agent is published again.
publish.askTheRoom: Where do the people you want to help already spend their day, and how would they find your agent there?
publish.sayOutLoud: Imagine Fabrikam builds a travel helper agent. Until it is published, only its builders can try it. After it is published and connected to a channel, employees with access can chat with it.

quiz.q: You edited a published agent but have not published again. What do channel users see?
quiz.why: Edits stay in draft until you publish again, so channel users keep the last published version.

options: A place where people reach the agent
quiz.why: A channel is where people talk to an agent, such as Teams or a website.

quiz.q: Which of these can stop you from using a channel?
options: Your organization's data policy or the agent's sign-in setting
The color of the agent's icon
quiz.why: Learn says a channel can be unavailable when a data policy or the sign-in configuration blocks it.

testing.definition: Testing shows how an agent behaves, either in a chat with you or by scoring many sample questions, before and after you publish.
testing.analogy: Think of it like a rehearsal plus a graded quiz: you try the agent by hand, then score it on a fixed set of questions.

blocks.label: Test chat
blocks.plain: A chat window where you talk to the agent as a user would.

blocks.label: Activity view
blocks.plain: Shows what the agent did, such as which tools and knowledge it used.

blocks.label: Test set
blocks.plain: A saved group of sample questions or conversations to run again and again.

blocks.label: Test method
blocks.plain: The rule that scores an answer, such as quality or content safety.

blocks.label: Results
blocks.plain: Scores and details for each test case, so you can compare runs.

flow.label: Try
flow.plain: You chat with the agent and watch how it answers.

flow.label: Look
flow.plain: You check what the agent did behind the scenes, not just what it said.

flow.label: Build set
flow.plain: You write, import, or generate a set of sample questions.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The product sends each question to the agent and records the answers.

flow.label: Score
flow.plain: Each answer is scored by the test methods you picked.

flow.label: Improve
flow.plain: You change the agent and run the same set again to compare.

example.input: A maker asks {sampleQuestion} in the test chat, then runs a saved set of similar questions after each change.
example.output: The chat shows how one answer reads and what the agent used. The run gives a result for each question and a summary for the whole set.

whenToUse: You want to see how the agent answers before people use it.
You changed instructions, knowledge, or tools and need to check nothing broke.
You need the same questions run the same way every time.
whenNot: Safety checks help find harmful content but do not guarantee safety.
Timers and background events may only work after you publish.
On usage-based harnesses, testing and evaluating can use Copilot Credits.
testing.dataNote: Evaluations run as the person who is signed in, using that person's access. In the standard harness, a saved snapshot of a test chat can hold all of the agent's content, which might include sensitive information.
testing.needToKnow: Testing has two jobs: chatting shows one conversation in detail, and a saved set of questions gives repeatable scores you can compare after each change. Use both for a full picture.
testing.demo: Chat with a sample agent and show what it did behind the scenes. Then show a saved set of questions with a score for each answer.
testing.askTheRoom: What would a wrong answer from your agent cost your team or your customers?
testing.sayOutLoud: Contoso changes one instruction and wonders if anything broke. Instead of asking questions by hand, the team runs the same saved questions before and after the change and compares the scores.

quiz.q: Why run the same saved set of questions again after you change the agent?
options: To compare results and see what got better or worse
quiz.why: Running the same test set gives you an objective standard to compare changes in performance.

quiz.q: What does the activity view help you see?
options: What the agent did, such as the tools and knowledge it used
Who will use the agent next month
How many people like the agent's name
quiz.why: The activity view shows how the agent handled a message, so you can tell where a wrong answer came from.

quiz.q: Can a safety test prove an agent is safe in every situation?
options: Yes, a pass means it is always safe
No, it helps find harmful content but is not a guarantee
Only if you run it once
quiz.why: Learn says content safety tests help identify harmful content but do not guarantee safety, so keep using responsible AI reviews.

monitor.definition: Monitoring shows how an agent is doing once people use it, so you can spot problems and decide what to improve.
monitor.analogy: Think of it like a car dashboard: it does not drive for you, but it shows speed, fuel, and warning lights.

blocks.label: Sessions
blocks.plain: Individual conversations or runs, with their length, channel, and status.

blocks.label: Outcomes
blocks.plain: How conversations ended, or how many runs succeeded or failed.

blocks.label: Feedback
blocks.plain: Thumbs up or down reactions and survey scores from users.

blocks.label: Tools and sources
blocks.plain: Which tools and knowledge the agent used, and how often they worked.

blocks.label: Usage and credits
blocks.plain: How often the agent is used and how many Copilot Credits it consumed.

flow.label: Go live
flow.plain: People start using the agent, and the product records each conversation or run.

flow.label: Collect
flow.plain: The product gathers outcomes, feedback, tool use, and credits over time.

flow.label: Refresh
flow.plain: Reports update after a delay, so very recent activity may not show yet.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You look at a time period and compare it with the one before.

flow.label: Drill in
flow.plain: You open individual sessions to read what was said and what the agent did.

flow.label: Improve
flow.plain: You fix instructions, knowledge, or tools, then watch the numbers again.

example.input: Contoso's help agent has been live for two weeks, and the team wants to know how it is doing.
example.output: A summary of sessions, how they ended, user reactions, tool use, and credits used. Drilling in shows which conversations failed or were handed to a person.

whenToUse: The agent is live and you want to know if it helps people.
You want to find failed or abandoned sessions to fix.
You need to watch usage and credit use over time.
whenNot: In the standard harness, test chat activity does not appear in reports.
Reports lag by a few hours, so they are not a live alarm.
Numbers show trends, not reasons. Read sessions to learn why.
monitor.dataNote: Reports can include conversation transcripts. In the standard harness, feedback data is stored in Dataverse, and reading transcripts needs a specific security role.
monitor.needToKnow: Monitoring shows what is happening in live use. Pair it with testing: reports show where to look, and tests show whether a fix worked. Reports can lag by a few hours.
monitor.demo: Show the monitoring view of an agent that has some history, with one session transcript.
monitor.askTheRoom: If you could see one number about your agent each week, which would you pick?
monitor.sayOutLoud: Fabrikam's agent has been live for a month. The team opens its monitoring view and sees that most chats end well, but many conversations about one subject end unfinished. That tells them where to improve first.

quiz.q: When does monitoring have real usage to show?
options: After people start using the published agent
Only after you move the agent to another environment
quiz.why: You can look at monitoring early, but production usage, feedback, and credit data appear after you publish and people use the agent.

quiz.q: Which question can monitoring help answer?
options: Are people finishing their conversations or giving up?
quiz.why: Outcomes such as resolved, escalated, and abandoned show whether conversations end well.

quiz.q: Why might a report not show a conversation from an hour ago?
quiz.why: Learn says some numbers refresh within hours, and AI-based numbers refresh daily or weekly.

security.definition: Security controls decide who can talk to an agent, what it can reach, and what it may say.
security.analogy: Think of it like a building with a front desk, keycards, and house rules: who gets in, which rooms they can enter, and how everyone behaves inside.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: Proof of who the person is before the agent shares private information.

blocks.label: Access
blocks.plain: Rules about who can use the agent and which content each person can reach.

blocks.label: Content filters
blocks.plain: Checks that limit harmful content in what the agent says.

blocks.label: Agent identity
blocks.plain: The account an agent uses to prove itself to channels and services.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person starts a conversation with the agent.

flow.label: Sign in
flow.plain: If sign-in is required, the person proves who they are first.

flow.label: Check access
flow.plain: The agent only uses content and tools that person is allowed to use.

flow.label: Filter
flow.plain: Safety filters check answers for harmful content and can block them.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The agent replies, or declines if the request is blocked or not allowed.

flow.label: Log
flow.plain: Sign-in and activity can be logged so admins can review what happened.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks an HR agent for their own pay details.
example.output: The agent asks the person to sign in, shows only what that person may see, and applies its safety filters before replying.

whenToUse: The agent reaches private or business data.
People outside your own team will use the agent.
You need to control which people and channels can reach the agent.
whenNot: Skipping sign-in lets anyone with the link chat. Avoid it for private data.
Stricter safety settings can mean fewer answers; looser ones raise the risk of harm.
security.needToKnow: Security answers three questions: who is the person, what may they reach, and what may the agent say. Each question has its own control. In the standard and Microsoft Copilot harnesses, changes to these settings take effect after you publish.
security.demo: Show how the agent treats a signed-in employee compared with a stranger.
security.askTheRoom: Which of your agent ideas would handle information you would not want a stranger to see?
security.sayOutLoud: Think of a Contoso benefits agent. It should know who is asking, show only what that person may see, and refuse unsafe requests. Those three jobs are what these controls cover.

quiz.q: What happens if an agent uses no sign-in at all?
options: Only your team can chat with it
Anyone who has the link can chat with it
quiz.why: Learn warns that with no authentication, anyone who has the link can chat with the agent.

quiz.q: Why does an agent respect each person's own permissions?
options: So people only get content they are already allowed to see
So the agent can skip safety checks
quiz.why: Knowledge sources that use the person's sign-in only surface content that the specific person can access.

quiz.q: What does a stricter safety setting usually mean?
options: Fewer answers and tighter filtering of harmful content
quiz.why: Learn says the highest moderation level gives fewer answers and a stricter filter, and the lowest gives the most answers with more risk.

governance.definition: Governance is how a company keeps agents in check: rules for what they may connect to, a list of agents, and safe ways to move them.
governance.analogy: Think of it like a company policy plus an asset list: the policy says what is allowed, and the list shows what you have.

blocks.label: Policies
blocks.plain: Admin rules that allow or block connectors, channels, and other features.

blocks.label: Environments
blocks.plain: Separate spaces where agents are built, tested, and used.

blocks.label: Solutions
blocks.plain: Packages that carry an agent from one environment to another.

blocks.label: Inventory
blocks.plain: A list of agents with owner, channels, and how they sign in.

blocks.label: Roles
blocks.plain: Permissions that decide who may build, share, or manage agents.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: A maker builds an agent in an environment the company manages.

flow.label: Policy check
flow.plain: Data policies are checked as the agent connects to services or channels.

flow.label: Package
flow.plain: The agent is added to a solution so it can move between environments.

flow.label: Move
flow.plain: You export the solution from one environment and import it in another.

flow.label: Record
flow.plain: The agent appears in the inventory with its owner and settings.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: Admins review the inventory and adjust policies as needs change.

example.input: Contoso wants makers to build agents but not publish them to certain channels.
example.output: An admin sets a data policy that blocks those channels. Makers see that the channel is unavailable, and the agent cannot be published there.

whenToUse: Many people build agents and you need one shared set of rules.
You move agents from a test space to a live space.
You must know which agents exist, who owns them, and what they reach.
whenNot: Rules cannot judge whether a single answer is good. Use testing for that.
Strict rules can block a channel or connector; makers then ask their administrator.
governance.dataNote: Data policies sort connectors into groups. Connectors in different groups cannot share data.
governance.needToKnow: Governance has two sides: controls that block risky choices, and records that show what exists. Solutions are the usual way to move an agent between environments, which is called application lifecycle management (ALM).
governance.demo: Show a data policy blocking a channel for an agent, then show that agent's entry in the inventory.
governance.askTheRoom: Who in your organization would need to approve a new agent before real customers use it?
governance.sayOutLoud: Fabrikam has fifty makers building agents. Without rules, nobody knows what each agent can reach. Governance gives IT one list of agents and a set of policies that apply everywhere.

quiz.q: What does a data policy do?
options: Limits which connectors and channels agents may use
quiz.why: Admins use data policies to govern how agents connect to data and services, including which channels they can publish to.

quiz.q: What is a solution used for?
options: Carrying an agent from one environment to another
quiz.why: A solution acts as a carrier for agents, so you can export it from one environment and import it into another.

quiz.q: What does an agent inventory help an admin see?
options: Which agents exist and how they are set up
quiz.why: The inventory lists agents with details such as who created them, channels, and how they sign in users.

billing.definition: Billing is how an agent's cost is measured, in units such as Copilot Credits, and how an organization pays for and limits that use.
billing.analogy: Think of it like a utility meter: usage is measured, and you decide how to pay and where to set limits.

blocks.label: Usage
blocks.plain: What the agent does: model work, tools, knowledge, and conversations.

blocks.label: Credits
blocks.plain: The unit that measures usage, called Copilot Credits.

blocks.label: Payment plan
blocks.plain: How credits are paid for, such as prepaid packs or pay-as-you-go.

blocks.label: Controls
blocks.plain: Limits and allocations that keep usage inside an agreed amount.

blocks.label: Reports
blocks.plain: Views of what each agent and environment used.

flow.label: Estimate
flow.plain: Before launch, a team forecasts credits with an estimator.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: Some harnesses charge while you build; others start after you publish.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: People use the agent, and each task or conversation uses credits.

flow.label: Measure
flow.plain: The product adds up credits by agent, environment, and tenant.

flow.label: Limit
flow.plain: Admins set allocations and monthly limits, and can stop an agent at its limit.

flow.label: Compare
flow.plain: Teams compare real use with the estimate and adjust.

example.input: Fabrikam plans a customer chat agent and wants to know what it will cost each month.
example.output: The team models expected volume in an estimator to forecast monthly credits, then compares the forecast with real use after launch. Estimates are not guarantees.

whenToUse: You need a budget before an agent goes live.
You want to compare a forecast with real use.
You need to keep one agent from using too much.
whenNot: An estimate is not a price quote or a promise of cost.
A limit on an environment covers every agent in it, not just one.
billing.needToKnow: On the Microsoft Copilot and Customer Conversation harnesses, credits are charged to the environment and agent, not to individual people. The Microsoft Copilot harness can use credits while you build and test. Each harness bills in its own way.
billing.demo: Show the usage estimator with a low and a high traffic level, then show where real credit use appears for an agent.
billing.askTheRoom: What would be a fair monthly budget for your first agent, and who would own it?
billing.sayOutLoud: Contoso builds a support agent. Each conversation uses credits, like minutes on a phone plan. The team estimates usage first, then watches real use and sets a monthly limit for the agent.

quiz.q: What does a Copilot Credit measure?
options: How much an agent is used
How long an agent has existed
How many people can sign in
quiz.why: Copilot Credits are the unit that measures agent usage.
Learn says the estimator gives informational estimates, and actual consumption depends on real use.

quiz.q: Compared with the standard harness, when can the Microsoft Copilot harness start using credits?
quiz.why: Learn says the standard harness starts billing after publish, while the Microsoft Copilot harness charges from the moment you start building.

quiz.q: Which of these helps keep one agent from using too many credits?
options: A monthly limit on that agent
quiz.why: Admins can set a monthly limit for an agent, with notices and an option to stop usage at the limit.

publish-agent.definition: In the standard harness, publishing applies your latest saved changes to every channel connected to the agent.

blocks.label: Test chat
blocks.plain: Always shows your latest changes while you build.

blocks.label: Published version
blocks.plain: What channel users get until you publish again.

blocks.label: Channels
blocks.plain: Every connected channel updates together when you publish.

blocks.label: Session
blocks.plain: A conversation. New content arrives when a new session starts.

flow.label: Edit
flow.plain: You change the agent, and the test chat shows the change at once.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: Publishing applies the changes to all connected channels and can take a few minutes.

flow.label: New session
flow.plain: Chats in progress keep the old content until a new session starts.

flow.label: Restart
flow.plain: In Teams-style chats, a person can type start over to begin a new session.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: You try the published agent yourself before sharing it widely.

example.input: A Contoso maker fixes a wrong answer in an agent that is already live in Teams.
example.output: After publishing, new conversations use the fix. A chat already in progress keeps the old answer until a new session starts.

whenToUse: You fixed or added content and want users to get it.
You want to try the published version yourself before sharing it.
whenNot: Do not make the agent widely available in Teams before it is tested.
Do not share the demo website link with customers.

learn.title: Key concepts - Publish and deploy your agent

mc-publish-agent.definition: In the Microsoft Copilot harness, publishing creates a new live version from your current draft, after readiness and data policy checks.

blocks.label: Draft
blocks.plain: Your working copy. It can keep changing after a publish.

blocks.label: Readiness
blocks.plain: Needs a name, description, and instructions. Blocking issues stop a publish; warnings do not.

blocks.label: Live version
blocks.plain: Each publish makes a new version of the agent.

blocks.label: Channels
blocks.plain: Learn lists Microsoft Copilot, Teams, a demo website, and a web app as available.

flow.label: Preview
flow.plain: You test the saved draft in the preview chat.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The product checks that the agent is ready and that your data policies allow it.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: A new live version is created, and a status shows progress.

flow.label: Distribute
flow.plain: You connect channels and share the agent so users can find it.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: Draft changes reach users only after the next publish.

flow.label: Retry
flow.plain: If publishing fails, the details show what to fix, and you can try again.

example.input: Contoso finishes a travel booking agent and wants staff to use it in Microsoft Copilot and Teams.
example.output: The product checks the name, description, and instructions, then creates a live version. Staff reach it through the channels you connect.

whenToUse: A draft is ready and tested in the preview chat.
You updated an agent and want users to get the new version.
You want a stable live version while the draft keeps changing.
whenNot: A missing name, description, or instructions blocks publishing.
A data policy can block a channel. Ask an administrator to review it.
mc-publish-agent.dataNote: Published agents still follow your data policies. The publish step checks them too.

learn.title: Publish overview for agents (Microsoft Copilot)
Publish an agent (Microsoft Copilot)

authentication.definition: User authentication lets people sign in so an agent can reach restricted information for them. Single sign-on (SSO) can skip a second sign-in.

blocks.label: No sign-in
blocks.plain: Anyone with the link can chat, and the agent reaches only public information.

blocks.label: Microsoft sign-in
blocks.plain: Sets up Microsoft Entra ID sign-in for Teams, SharePoint, Power Apps, and Microsoft Copilot.

blocks.label: Manual sign-in
blocks.plain: Lets you use Microsoft Entra ID or another standard OAuth 2.0 provider.

blocks.label: Single sign-on
blocks.plain: Skips a second sign-in when the person is already signed in to the page.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: A person starts chatting with the agent in a channel.

flow.label: Sign in
flow.plain: If sign-in is required, the person signs in with the chosen provider.

flow.label: Identify
flow.plain: The agent learns who the person is, such as their name.

flow.label: Use access
flow.plain: Tools and knowledge that need the person's credentials work for that person.

flow.label: Skip repeat
flow.plain: With single sign-on set up, a person already signed in is not asked again.

example.input: A Fabrikam employee chats with an HR agent in Teams.
example.output: With Microsoft sign-in, Teams users are not asked to sign in unless the agent needs more access. The agent can then reach what that employee may see.

whenToUse: The agent reads or changes private data for each person.
Only people in your organization should use the agent.
Your website already signs customers in.
whenNot: No sign-in suits only public information.
Automated evaluations do not support manual sign-in.

learn.title: Configure user authentication in Copilot Studio
Configure single sign-on with Microsoft Entra ID

dlp-governance.definition: Data policies let admins sort connectors into groups and limit what agents can connect to or publish to.

blocks.label: Data groups
blocks.plain: Business, non-business, and blocked groups sort the connectors.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.plain: The environments a policy applies to.

blocks.label: Agent rules
blocks.plain: Limits on sign-in, tools, web requests, channels, and triggers.

blocks.label: Real-time check
blocks.plain: Makers and users see an error when a rule is broken.

flow.label: Admin sets
flow.plain: An admin builds a policy that groups connectors and covers chosen environments.

flow.label: Maker builds
flow.plain: A maker adds connectors, tools, or channels to an agent.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The policy is checked in real time as the agent is built and published.

flow.label: Block
flow.plain: A blocked item shows as unavailable, or an error explains the problem.

flow.label: Fix
flow.plain: The maker picks an allowed option or asks an admin to review the policy.

example.input: Contoso wants every agent to require sign-in before it can be published.
example.output: An admin blocks the connector that allows chat without sign-in. Makers can then use only Microsoft sign-in or manual sign-in.

whenToUse: You must keep business data away from personal or public services.
You want to block certain channels, web requests, or event triggers.
Many makers build agents in shared environments.
whenNot: A policy does not allow mixing connectors from different data groups.
Makers cannot override a block. They need an admin to change the policy.
dlp-governance.dataNote: Data policies sort connectors into groups. Connectors in different groups cannot share data.

learn.title: Configure data policies for agents

alm-solutions.definition: A solution is a package that carries an agent and its parts from one environment to another, such as from testing to live use.

blocks.label: Solution
blocks.plain: The package that carries the agent.

blocks.label: Required parts
blocks.plain: Flows, custom connectors, and variables the agent needs must be added too.

blocks.label: Export and import
blocks.plain: A solution file leaves one environment and arrives in another.

blocks.label: After import
blocks.plain: Sign-in is set up again, and the agent is published before it is shared.

flow.label: Package
flow.plain: The agent is added to a solution you can carry between environments.

flow.label: Add parts
flow.plain: Flows, custom connectors, and variables are added so nothing is missing.

flow.label: Export
flow.plain: The solution leaves the source environment as a file.

flow.label: Import
flow.plain: The solution is brought into the target environment.

flow.label: Set up
flow.plain: Sign-in is set up again, and the agent is published before it is shared.

example.input: Fabrikam builds an agent in a test environment and needs it in production.
example.output: The team adds the agent and its flows to a solution, exports it, imports it into production, sets up sign-in again, and publishes.

whenToUse: You use separate environments for testing and live use.
You need to move or back up an agent between environments.
You want to automate moving agents between environments.
whenNot: Not every part comes across. Comments and some channel details stay behind.
A managed solution cannot be exported from Copilot Studio.

learn.title: Create and manage solutions in Copilot Studio
Export and import agents using solutions

analytics.definition: In the standard harness, the monitoring page shows how an agent is doing, from outcomes to feedback to tool use.

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.plain: Key numbers, such as active users, with change from the last period.

blocks.label: Effectiveness
blocks.plain: Outcomes, reactions, satisfaction scores, and sentiment.

blocks.label: Use
blocks.plain: Themes, answer quality, tool use, and knowledge source use.

blocks.label: Sessions
blocks.plain: Lists of sessions and questions you can drill into.

flow.label: Users chat
flow.plain: People talk to the published agent, and sessions are recorded.

flow.label: Classify
flow.plain: Each engaged session ends as resolved, escalated, or abandoned.

flow.label: Feedback
flow.plain: Reactions and survey answers add what users think.

flow.label: Refresh
flow.plain: Most numbers refresh within hours. AI-based ones refresh daily or weekly.

flow.label: Drill in
flow.plain: You open lists of questions and sessions to find weak spots.

example.input: Contoso's agent has been live for a month.
example.output: The page shows how sessions ended, what users thought, and which topics, tools, and knowledge were used.

whenToUse: You want to see where conversations succeed or break down.
You want to know which knowledge sources and tools help most.
You need ideas for which topics to improve first.
whenNot: Active user counts need the agent to require sign-in.
Test chat activity does not appear in reports.
Session details and transcripts cover the last 28 days.

learn.title: Monitor agent performance in Copilot Studio
Monitor conversational agent effectiveness

test-agent.definition: The test chat lets you talk to a standard harness agent as a user would, and see which steps ran and what values they held.

blocks.label: Test chat
blocks.plain: A panel where you chat with the agent as a user would.

blocks.label: Fired steps
blocks.plain: Steps that ran are marked, so you can follow the path.

blocks.label: Variable values
blocks.plain: Shows the values the agent held during the chat.

blocks.label: Activity map
blocks.plain: Shows the plan of a generative agent as it happens.

blocks.label: Snapshot
blocks.plain: A saved file of the conversation and its diagnostics.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: You type a question the way a user would.

flow.label: Match
flow.plain: The agent starts a topic, or plans which topics, tools, and knowledge to use.

flow.label: Follow
flow.plain: You follow the path the conversation took through topics and steps.

flow.label: Inspect
flow.plain: You watch variable values change as the chat goes on.

flow.label: Reset
flow.plain: You start a new test session to clear the old conversation.

example.input: A Contoso maker asks {sampleQuestion} and wants to see why the agent answered that way.
example.output: The chat shows the answer. The map and the marked steps show which topic, tool, or knowledge the agent used to get there.

whenToUse: You are building topics and want to see them run.
You need to find out why an answer went wrong.
You want to check variable values mid-conversation.
whenNot: The test chat does not fully copy published channels.
Use test sets when you need to run many questions at once.
test-agent.dataNote: A saved snapshot holds all of the agent's content, which might include sensitive information.

learn.title: Test your agent

evaluations.definition: Agent evaluation runs a saved set of test questions on your agent and scores each answer, so you can compare after every change.

blocks.label: Test case
blocks.plain: One question or conversation, sometimes with the answer you expect.

blocks.label: Test set
blocks.plain: A group of test cases you can run again.

blocks.label: Test methods
blocks.plain: How answers are scored: quality, meaning, keywords, safety, and more.

blocks.label: Results
blocks.plain: A result for each case and a pass rate for the set.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: You generate, import, or write test cases.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: You pick test methods. General quality is there by default.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The questions are sent to the agent, and the answers are recorded.

flow.label: Score
flow.plain: Each case gets pass, fail, invalid, or error.

flow.label: Compare
flow.plain: You run the same set again and see what improved or got worse.

example.input: A maker checks that the agent answers a question about business hours with the right hours.
example.output: The test case holds the question and the expected answer. After a run, the maker sees pass or fail, the reasoning, and what the agent used.

whenToUse: You want repeatable quality checks, not one chat at a time.
You changed the agent and want to compare scores.
You want to check answers for harmful content.
whenNot: Evaluations support only no sign-in or Microsoft sign-in.
Only one evaluation can run at a time.
Results stay for 89 days, so export them to keep them longer.
evaluations.dataNote: Evaluations run as the person who is signed in, using that person's access.

learn.title: About agent evaluation
Choose evaluation methods

mc-credit-billing.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, building, testing, and running an agent can use Copilot Credits, and admins can allocate, limit, and track them.

blocks.label: Credits
blocks.plain: Cover model tokens, tools, knowledge, and the harness itself.

blocks.label: Not included
blocks.plain: This usage is not part of a Microsoft 365 Copilot license.

blocks.label: Allocation
blocks.plain: Admins can give an environment a set amount of prepaid credits.

blocks.label: Agent limit
blocks.plain: A monthly limit can warn about one agent or stop it.

blocks.label: Reports
blocks.plain: Monitor shows credits per agent. Admin reports show tenant and environment use.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: Creating an agent with natural language uses credits.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: Preview chats and evaluations show running estimates of credits.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: Each task people give the agent uses credits.

flow.label: Total
flow.plain: Monitor shows the final total used for billing, not an early estimate.

flow.label: Control
flow.plain: Admins allocate credits and set limits to stay within a plan.

example.input: Fabrikam makers are building many Microsoft Copilot harness agents in one environment.
example.output: An admin gives that environment prepaid credits and sets a monthly limit for an agent. Notices warn when usage nears a limit.

whenToUse: You are planning usage for agents in a shared environment.
You want makers to explore inside a spending boundary.
whenNot: Agent limits do not cap the total use of an environment.
Azure budgets send alerts but do not stop usage.

learn.title: Overview of usage-based billing
Manage costs for agents powered by the Microsoft Copilot harness

usage-credits.definition: The estimator forecasts the Copilot Credits your agents will need each month, and monitoring later shows real use to compare.

blocks.label: Inputs
blocks.plain: Agent type, traffic, orchestration, knowledge, and tools shape the estimate.

blocks.label: Estimate
blocks.plain: A forecast with a breakdown by activity, such as knowledge and actions.

blocks.label: Export
blocks.plain: A PDF report for budget and purchase reviews.

blocks.label: Real use
blocks.plain: Reports show the real credits used after launch.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: You enter agent types, traffic, and features.

flow.label: Estimate
flow.plain: The tool adds up the monthly credits for each agent.

flow.label: Add buffer
flow.plain: Learn advises adding a 10 to 20 percent buffer to the estimate.

flow.label: Launch
flow.plain: The agent runs, and real credits are recorded.

flow.label: Compare
flow.plain: You compare the forecast with actual use and adjust.

example.input: Fabrikam expects heavy chat traffic during a holiday sale.
example.output: The team tests low, medium, and high volume cases and exports a report. After launch, they compare actual credits with the forecast.

whenToUse: You need a budget before buying credits.
You want to compare different agent setups.
You are adding up costs for several agents.
whenNot: The estimator is not a price quote or a guarantee.
It looks forward only. It does not track past use.

learn.title: Agent usage estimator
View agent's billing consumption

content-moderation.definition: Content moderation filters what an agent says for harmful content. A stricter level blocks more harmful content but can mean fewer answers.

blocks.label: Moderation level
blocks.plain: A scale from lowest to highest that sets how strict filtering is.

blocks.label: Where set
blocks.plain: Agent, topic, or prompt level. The topic setting wins at run time.

blocks.label: Grounding rule
blocks.plain: A setting can block answers that used no knowledge or tools.

blocks.label: Safety tests
blocks.plain: Evaluations can check answers for hate, sexual content, violence, and self-harm.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person sends a message to the agent.

flow.label: Generate
flow.plain: The model drafts an answer from knowledge, tools, and instructions.

flow.label: Filter
flow.plain: Moderation checks the answer against the harm categories.

flow.label: Block or show
flow.plain: Blocked content gives no answer and no notice. Safe content is shown.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: Evaluations with safety methods help you check the result.

example.input: A maker wants the Fabrikam help agent to be careful with harmful requests.
example.output: A stricter level gives fewer answers and filters harmful content more. Safety tests then help check the result, but no test guarantees safety.

whenToUse: The agent answers open questions from knowledge sources.
Real customers, not just your team, will use the agent.
You want to check safety before and after you publish.
whenNot: Lower levels allow more answers but raise the risk of harmful content.
The prompt-level slider is not available for some model types.
content-moderation.dataNote: When content is moderated, the agent may give no answer and no notice. Moderation events can be logged if the agent is connected to Application Insights.

learn.title: Knowledge sources summary
Choose evaluation methods

channel-teams.definition: A published agent can be added to Teams and Microsoft Copilot, so people can install it and chat with it there.

blocks.label: Published agent
blocks.plain: Publish at least once before Teams can use it.

blocks.label: Appearance
blocks.plain: The icon, color, and descriptions people see in the store.

blocks.label: Sharing
blocks.plain: An install link, or a share with people and groups.

blocks.label: Admin approval
blocks.plain: An approved agent is listed as built by your organization.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The agent is published at least once.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: You connect the Teams and Microsoft 365 channel. Microsoft Copilot is optional.

flow.label: Install
flow.plain: You install the agent for yourself first.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: Others install from a link or find it in the agent store.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: New content shows in new conversations. A chat can restart to see it.

example.input: Contoso publishes an HR agent and wants employees to ask it questions in Teams.
example.output: The maker connects the channel, installs the agent first, then shares it. Employees need access to the agent to chat with it.

whenToUse: Your people already work in Teams or Microsoft Copilot.
You want to share an install link with a team.
You want the agent listed for the whole organization.
whenNot: A link alone gives no access. People must also be shared on the agent.
People who installed from a link must reinstall to see changed details.

learn.title: Connect and configure an agent for Teams and Microsoft Copilot

voice-agents.definition: A real-time voice agent talks with callers in a natural way, and topics can add fixed rules such as greetings and handoff.

blocks.label: Voice model
blocks.plain: A real-time speech model, or a text model with a synthesized voice.

blocks.label: Topics
blocks.plain: Fixed rules for greetings, business rules, and handoff.

blocks.label: Contact center
blocks.plain: Voice runs over Dynamics 365 Contact Center channels.

blocks.label: Caller input
blocks.plain: Speech and keypad tones, with interruptions allowed.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: A caller reaches the agent through a voice channel.

flow.label: Listen
flow.plain: The model hears the caller, and the caller can interrupt it.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The model answers, or a topic handles a fixed rule.

flow.label: Act
flow.plain: The agent can use knowledge and tools, or hand the caller to a person.

example.input: A Fabrikam customer calls to ask about an order.
example.output: The agent understands the request without menu choices, uses connected knowledge or tools, and can hand the caller to a person when needed.

whenToUse: Customers prefer to call and talk instead of using menus.
You need both natural talk and fixed rules, such as escalation.
whenNot: A real-time voice agent cannot switch back to a basic voice agent.
Voice needs Dynamics 365 Contact Center set up first.
voice-agents.dataNote: Some real-time voice models can process data outside the AI resource's Azure region. Data storage stays in that region.

learn.title: Real-time agents overview
Configure real-time agents

cc-deploy-channels.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, one place publishes the agent and connects it to channels, starting with a demo website made for you.

blocks.label: Demo website
blocks.plain: A prebuilt site for testing. Do not share it with customers.

blocks.label: Web chat
blocks.plain: Puts the agent on your own website with a script.

blocks.label: Teams Phone
blocks.plain: Lets customers call the agent on a phone number.

blocks.label: Contact center
blocks.plain: Dynamics 365 Contact Center, Genesys, or your own platform.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: Publishing creates a demo website for you.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: Teammates try the agent on the demo website.

flow.label: Guide
flow.plain: The demo welcome message tells testers what to try.

flow.label: Go live
flow.plain: A script adds web chat to the live website.

flow.label: Add phone
flow.plain: Teams Phone needs a Teams admin to add a number and license.

example.input: Fabrikam wants customers to chat with an agent on its support page.
example.output: The team tests on the demo website, then a web developer adds the web chat script to the live page.

whenToUse: Customers will chat on a website or call a phone number.
You want teammates to test before customers see the agent.
whenNot: The demo website is not for production use.
Some contact center channels need an environment with Dynamics 365 apps.

learn.title: Deploy overview (Customer Conversation)
Deploy an agent (Customer Conversation)

cc-teams-phone.definition: Teams Phone lets customers call the agent on a Teams phone number, set up by a maker and a Teams admin.

blocks.label: Maker
blocks.plain: Turns the channel on for the agent.

blocks.label: Resource account
blocks.plain: The agent's account, which the Teams admin sees.

blocks.label: Teams admin
blocks.plain: Adds a phone number and a license.

blocks.label: Licenses
blocks.plain: Needs Copilot Studio and Teams Phone licenses.

flow.label: Enable
flow.plain: The maker enables the Teams Phone channel for the agent.

flow.label: Hand off
flow.plain: The maker tells the Teams admin which agent to set up.

flow.label: Provision
flow.plain: The admin sets up a phone number and a license.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: Customers call the number and reach the voice agent.

example.input: Fabrikam wants customers to call and check an order status.
example.output: The maker enables the channel and hands off to a Teams admin, who adds the number. Customers then call and reach the voice agent.

whenToUse: Customers want to call a phone number and talk to the agent.
You need specialized call flows, such as billing or order status.
whenNot: Admins can turn off the Teams Phone channel for agents.
Setup involves two roles, a maker and a Teams admin.

learn.title: Deploy an agent (Customer Conversation)

mc-preview-test.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, the preview chat lets you talk to your draft agent, read its activity trace, and see a running credit estimate.

blocks.label: Preview chat
blocks.plain: A chat that mirrors how users talk to the published agent.

blocks.label: Activity trace
blocks.plain: Shows reasoning steps, knowledge used, tools run, and errors.

blocks.label: History
blocks.plain: Past test conversations you can review and filter.

blocks.label: Credit estimate
blocks.plain: A running total of estimated Copilot Credits for the test.

flow.label: Chat
flow.plain: You send messages and read the replies in real time.

flow.label: Trace
flow.plain: The trace shows how the agent handled each message.

flow.label: Rate
flow.plain: You rate replies with thumbs up or down and add comments.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You look back at earlier test conversations.

flow.label: Estimate
flow.plain: The credit estimate shows what testing costs.

example.input: A maker asks {sampleQuestion} and wants to know where the answer came from.
example.output: The reply appears in the chat. The trace shows the knowledge sources and tools the agent used to produce it.

whenToUse: You are iterating on instructions or knowledge.
You need to debug one reply or one tool call.
whenNot: Preview does not replace saved test sets for many questions.
Testing can use Copilot Credits.

learn.title: Preview and test an agent (Microsoft Copilot)

mc-evaluate.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, an evaluation scores your agent on test conversations with the methods you pick, then compares runs after changes.

blocks.label: Conversations
blocks.plain: Test cases with user messages and, optionally, expected replies.

blocks.label: Evaluation
blocks.plain: A named test set with up to five test methods.

blocks.label: Test methods
blocks.plain: General quality, safety, meaning, tool use, keywords, and more.

blocks.label: Credit estimate
blocks.plain: Shows estimated credits for generating and scoring answers.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: You make an evaluation and add conversations.

flow.label: Method
flow.plain: You pick test methods. A new evaluation starts with general quality.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The evaluation runs against the agent version you picked.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You read scores and find weak spots.

flow.label: Iterate
flow.plain: You change the agent and run again to measure the effect.

example.input: A maker changed the instructions of an agent and wants to know if answers got better.
example.output: The maker runs the same evaluation again and compares the new scores with the old ones, and sees the credits the run used.

whenToUse: You want repeatable quality checks before you publish.
You need to know if a change made answers better or worse.
whenNot: This feature is in preview, so details can change.
Agents set to manual sign-in are not supported.

learn.title: Evaluate an agent (preview)

cc-preview-test.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, you test the saved agent in web chat and by voice call, and use an activity map to see what it did.

blocks.label: Web chat
blocks.plain: A text chat, where most testing time should go.

blocks.label: Voice call
blocks.plain: A live voice test that finds problems text cannot.

blocks.label: Activity map
blocks.plain: Shows routing, tool calls, and topic runs.

blocks.label: Break tests
blocks.plain: Tests that push the agent to fail on purpose, to see it fail safely.

flow.label: Happy path
flow.plain: You play a realistic user with a complete goal.

flow.label: Break it
flow.plain: You skip details, change your mind, or ask something out of scope.

flow.label: Read map
flow.plain: The activity map shows where a wrong answer came from.

flow.label: Voice
flow.plain: You test voice separately, including interruptions and silence.

flow.label: Retest
flow.plain: You fix one thing, start a new session, and run it again.

example.input: A Fabrikam maker tests a travel agent by booking a trip, then asks about something out of scope.
example.output: The agent should finish the booking, then decline the out-of-scope request and steer back to its job.

whenToUse: You want to test chat and voice before customers do.
You need to find out whether routing or a tool caused a wrong answer.
whenNot: Preview runs the saved agent, not unsaved edits.
Chat passing does not cover voice. Test voice separately.

learn.title: Preview and test an agent (Customer Conversation)

cc-evaluate.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, a test set is run against the draft or the published agent and scored with up to five test methods.

blocks.label: Test set
blocks.plain: Single questions, or longer conversations (preview).

blocks.label: Data source
blocks.plain: Questions come from a file, are generated, or are written by you.

blocks.label: Test methods
blocks.plain: General quality, meaning, keywords, text similarity, and more.

blocks.label: User profile
blocks.plain: An account with connections, so tools can be tested too.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: You make a test set from a file, by generating, or by writing.

flow.label: Configure
flow.plain: You name it, pick test methods, and choose the agent version.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The questions run against the draft or the published agent.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You read the results to see how the agent did.

example.input: A Contoso team wants to check a support agent before it goes live.
example.output: The team builds a test set of customer questions, runs it against the draft, and reads which answers passed or failed.

whenToUse: You want to measure quality on a batch of questions.
You want to test the draft before you publish.
whenNot: Conversation test sets are in preview.
Generated question sets reach up to 100 questions.

learn.title: Evaluate an agent (Customer Conversation)

multiturn-tests.definition: A conversation test set checks if an agent keeps context, asks questions when needed, and finishes tasks over a longer chat.

blocks.label: Test case
blocks.plain: One conversation of up to 12 messages.

blocks.label: Test set
blocks.plain: Up to 20 test cases in one set.

blocks.label: Methods
blocks.plain: General quality, content safety, keyword match, tool use, or custom.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: You generate conversations, import a spreadsheet, or reuse a test chat.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: You pick the test methods for the set.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: Each conversation is played against the agent.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You read the result and reasoning for each conversation.

example.input: A maker wants to know if an agent remembers a customer's earlier answer later in the chat.
example.output: A conversation test case plays several messages in a row. The result shows whether the agent kept context and finished the task.

whenToUse: Your agent must remember earlier answers in a chat.
You want to test clarifying questions and multi-step tasks.
whenNot: Compare meaning, text similarity, and exact match work only on single answers.
You have less control over conversations than in the test chat.

learn.title: Create a conversational test set

readiness-scorecard.definition: Evaluation results can be exported so a team can review the proof for each question before it releases an agent.

blocks.label: Exported results
blocks.plain: A file with each question, answer, method, result, and analysis.

blocks.label: Readiness warnings
blocks.plain: A review panel can warn that an agent has no evaluation yet.

blocks.label: Success rule
blocks.plain: Your team defines what good enough looks like before testing.

flow.label: Define
flow.plain: The team decides what success looks like before running tests.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The agent is evaluated with the same test set each time.

flow.label: Export
flow.plain: Results are exported to a file for review.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: The team reads the results and any readiness warnings together.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The team decides whether to release or keep improving.

example.input: Contoso wants proof before an agent goes live.
example.output: The team runs its test set, exports the results, and reviews each failed case. Warnings do not block publishing, so the team sets its own bar.

whenToUse: You want a record of how the agent did before release.
You want to compare runs before and after a change.
whenNot: Learn defines no release scorecard. The go or no-go rule is your team's call.
Results stay in the product for 89 days, so export them.

learn.title: Run evaluations and view results
About agent evaluation

mc-monitor.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, monitoring shows sessions, success and fail rates, reactions, tool use, and the credits the agent used.

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.plain: Total sessions, users, runs, average duration, and success rate.

blocks.label: Reactions
blocks.plain: Thumbs up and thumbs down feedback on replies.

blocks.label: Credits
blocks.plain: Total estimated credits, with a split by experience when available.

blocks.label: Sessions
blocks.plain: A list with status, duration, tools used, and credits.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: People use the published agent, and sessions are recorded.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You pick a period and compare it with the one before.

flow.label: Filter
flow.plain: You filter sessions by status to find failed ones.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: You open a session to see messages, tools, and knowledge used.

flow.label: Improve
flow.plain: You fix what you find and watch the numbers again.

example.input: A Fabrikam team wants to know why some sessions of its agent fail.
example.output: The team filters sessions by failed status, reads the transcripts, and checks for tool connection or sign-in errors.

whenToUse: You want one maker view of an agent's health.
You need to find failed sessions and see their credits.
whenNot: Real usage appears only after you publish and people use the agent.
The session list shows only the last 28 days.

learn.title: Monitor agent performance overview (Microsoft Copilot)

cc-monitor.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, monitoring shows how conversations ended, how good answers were, how tools and knowledge were used, and credits billed.

blocks.label: Outcomes
blocks.plain: Conversations sorted as resolved, escalated, abandoned, or unengaged.

blocks.label: Answer quality
blocks.plain: Counts of answered questions, rated for how good they are.

blocks.label: Tools and sources
blocks.plain: Tool success rates and which knowledge sources were used.

blocks.label: Billing
blocks.plain: The Copilot Credits billed for the chosen period.

flow.label: Deploy
flow.plain: Customers use the agent, and conversations are recorded.

flow.label: Summarize
flow.plain: An AI summary points out changes, such as session volume.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You check outcomes, satisfaction, sentiment, and answer quality.

flow.label: Drill in
flow.plain: You open questions and sessions behind a number.

flow.label: Download
flow.plain: You can download transcripts once a conversation times out.

example.input: A Contoso team wants to see how a support agent handles customer calls and chats.
example.output: The team sees how many conversations resolved or escalated, how good the answers were, and how many credits were billed.

whenToUse: Your agent is deployed and handling customer conversations.
You want to see which knowledge sources answer questions.
whenNot: Satisfaction and sentiment panels need enough responses first.
Custom metrics are still in preview.

learn.title: Monitor an agent (Customer Conversation)

entra-agent-identities.definition: An agent identity is a Microsoft Entra account that lets one agent prove who it is to channels and services.

blocks.label: Agent identity
blocks.plain: A special Microsoft Entra account for the agent, made for you.

blocks.label: Sponsor
blocks.plain: The agent owner is added for accountability.

blocks.label: Connector scopes
blocks.plain: Entra shows which connectors the agent is set up to use.

blocks.label: Visibility
blocks.plain: Admins can watch the agent's sign-in activity in Microsoft Entra.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: Copilot Studio creates the identity. When depends on the harness.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: Publishing attaches permissions for the connectors the agent uses.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The agent uses the identity to prove itself to channels and services.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: Admins check its sign-ins and risk state in Microsoft Entra.

flow.label: Delete
flow.plain: Deleting the agent removes its identity.

example.input: A Contoso admin wants to know which agents can reach a connector.
example.output: In Microsoft Entra, the admin sees each agent's identity and the connectors it can use.

whenToUse: You need to see which agents exist in Microsoft Entra.
You need to know what an agent is set up to reach.
whenNot: Makers cannot bring their own agent identity.
Today, rules on the identity are enforced at run time only in Teams.
entra-agent-identities.dataNote: Learn says no one in your tenant, including tenant admins, can generate tokens with an Entra Agent ID. Microsoft controls the mechanism.

learn.title: Agent identities and authentication for Copilot Studio
What are agent identities

mc-agent-settings-security.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, one settings area covers moderation, sign-in, feedback, and the greeting.

blocks.label: Moderation level
blocks.plain: Five levels, from minimum to maximum, set how strict filtering is.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: No authentication, or Microsoft sign-in.

blocks.label: Web channel security
blocks.plain: Secrets that protect requests coming from a website.

blocks.label: User feedback
blocks.plain: Thumbs up and down on each reply.

blocks.label: Greeting
blocks.plain: The first message and the suggested prompts.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: You decide how strict filtering and sign-in should be.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: You save the settings.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The settings take effect after you save and publish.

flow.label: Users
flow.plain: People see the greeting and can rate replies.

flow.label: Watch
flow.plain: Reactions show up in monitoring when feedback is on.

example.input: A Fabrikam maker wants an internal agent that signs staff in and filters carefully.
example.output: The maker picks Microsoft sign-in and a higher moderation level, saves, and publishes. The settings apply to the live agent after that.

whenToUse: You need to set how strict filtering and sign-in are.
You want users to rate replies.
whenNot: Manual sign-in is not supported on this harness.
Some identity details can only be set before the first save.

learn.title: Configure settings for agents powered by the Microsoft Copilot harness

cc-authentication.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, sign-in and voice authentication are set once and apply to every agent in the orchestration.

blocks.label: Sign-in mode
blocks.plain: How users sign in to all agents in the orchestration.

blocks.label: Voice authentication
blocks.plain: Requires caller verification on voice channels.

blocks.label: Dynamics 365 apps
blocks.plain: Voice authentication needs an environment where Dynamics 365 apps are turned on.

blocks.label: Details options
blocks.plain: Settings for ungrounded answers, web information, and file uploads.

flow.label: Pick mode
flow.plain: A maker picks how users sign in for the whole orchestration.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: On a voice channel, a caller reaches the agent.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The caller is checked with biometrics, policies, and one-time passcodes.

flow.label: Proceed
flow.plain: The agent continues once the caller is verified.

example.input: A Fabrikam customer calls about account details.
example.output: With voice authentication on, the caller is verified first. The same rule applies to every agent in the setup.

whenToUse: Callers must be verified before the agent shares account details.
You want one sign-in rule for all agents in the orchestration.
whenNot: Speech channels do not support end-user sign-in. Sign-in knowledge works for chat only.
Voice authentication needs an environment where Dynamics 365 apps are turned on.

learn.title: Configure agent details and security (Customer Conversation)

cc-biometric-auth.definition: Biometric authentication checks a caller by voice, so the agent knows who is calling before it shares details.

blocks.label: Identifier
blocks.plain: The details used to find the caller, such as a phone number.

blocks.label: Lookup table
blocks.plain: The table of customer records that matches the caller.

blocks.label: Authentication policy
blocks.plain: Sets how strong the check must be.

blocks.label: Condition
blocks.plain: A check that the caller passed before other tools run.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: A customer calls the voice agent.

flow.label: Identify
flow.plain: The agent finds the matching customer record.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The caller is checked against the chosen policy.

flow.label: Gate
flow.plain: Other tools and actions run only if verification passed.

example.input: A Contoso customer calls to change account details.
example.output: The agent identifies the caller from the call, verifies the caller, and only then runs tools that touch the account.

whenToUse: Callers must be verified before the agent discusses account details.
You want a smoother identity check for callers.
whenNot: Voice biometrics uses extra Copilot Credits.
It needs an environment with Dynamics 365 apps.
cc-biometric-auth.dataNote: Voice biometrics can fall under biometric and privacy laws. Learn says you are responsible for notice, consent, and how that data is handled.

learn.title: Prebuilt contact center tools (Customer Conversation)
Biometric authentication overview

agent-inventory.definition: The agent inventory gives IT and security admins one list of all agents made in Copilot Studio or Agent Builder, with their key details.

blocks.label: Inventory
blocks.plain: A central list of draft and published agents in the tenant.

blocks.label: Properties
blocks.plain: Creator, owner, last published, channels, and sign-in type.

blocks.label: Capabilities
blocks.plain: The connectors used, and whether web search is on.

blocks.label: Access
blocks.plain: Admins read it in the admin center or with code and queries.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: Makers create and publish agents across the tenant.

flow.label: Refresh
flow.plain: The inventory updates on its own, and changes usually show within 20 minutes.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: Admins look at who made each agent and what it can reach.

flow.label: Follow up
flow.plain: Admins act on owners and risks, then adjust policies.

example.input: A Contoso admin wants to know which agents are published to Teams and which are not signed in.
example.output: The inventory lists each agent with its channels and sign-in mode, so the admin can find agents that need attention.

whenToUse: You need to know which agents exist and who owns them.
You want to find agents with no sign-in or risky connectors.
whenNot: The inventory shows the published version, not unpublished edits.
It does not include classic chatbots, and some properties are in preview.

learn.title: Microsoft Copilot Studio Agent inventory

cc-export-import.definition: An agent on the Customer Conversation harness moves between environments in an unmanaged solution, and some parts do not come along.

blocks.label: Solution
blocks.plain: The package that carries the agent.

blocks.label: Extra parts
blocks.plain: Flows, custom connectors, and variables must be added too.

blocks.label: Left behind
blocks.plain: Comments, the conversation ID, and sometimes the icon or channel details.

blocks.label: After import
blocks.plain: Sign-in is set up again, and the agent is deployed before it is shared.

flow.label: Package
flow.plain: The agent is added to an unmanaged solution.

flow.label: Export
flow.plain: The solution is exported from the source environment.

flow.label: Import
flow.plain: The solution is imported into the target environment.

flow.label: Set up
flow.plain: Sign-in is set up again, and the agent is deployed.

example.input: Fabrikam needs its agent in an environment with Dynamics 365 apps for a contact center channel.
example.output: The team exports the agent in a solution, imports it there, sets up sign-in again, and deploys it.

whenToUse: A channel or feature needs a different environment.
You move an agent from testing to live use.
whenNot: A managed solution cannot be exported.
The imported agent may be missing its icon or channel details.

learn.title: Export and import an agent (Customer Conversation)

cc-credit-billing.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, each customer conversation uses Copilot Credits based on how complex it is and how it takes place.

blocks.label: Complexity
blocks.plain: Conversations are light, medium, or heavy, and use different credits.

blocks.label: Modality
blocks.plain: Digital chat, GenAI voice, and premium voice use different amounts.

blocks.label: Voice biometrics
blocks.plain: Adds credits for each enrollment or authentication check.

blocks.label: Admin controls
blocks.plain: Allocation, monthly agent limits, and usage reports.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: Admins plan for light, medium, and heavy conversations.

flow.label: Talk
flow.plain: Customers talk to the agent, and each conversation uses credits.

flow.label: Watch
flow.plain: Monitoring shows credits for an agent. Admin reports show more.

flow.label: Limit
flow.plain: Admins set agent limits, and can stop usage at a limit.

flow.label: Compare
flow.plain: Real use is compared with the estimate, and settings are adjusted.

example.input: Contoso plans a customer support agent for chat and voice.
example.output: An admin estimates the conversations and sets a monthly limit for the agent. Later, real credits are compared with the estimate.

whenToUse: You are planning capacity for customer conversations.
You use voice biometrics and need to count its credits.
whenNot: This usage is not covered by a Microsoft 365 Copilot license.
Costs are tracked by environment and agent, not by user.

learn.title: Overview of usage-based billing
Manage costs for agents powered by the Customer Conversation harness

fdy-publish-agent-copilot-teams.definition: Publishing a Foundry agent adds its stable address to Microsoft Copilot and Teams, so people can find and use it.

blocks.label: Active version
blocks.plain: The agent version that people reach through the stable address.

blocks.label: Publish scope
blocks.plain: Just you, or people in your organization.

blocks.label: Admin approval
blocks.plain: An admin must approve company-wide publishing.

blocks.label: Store listing
blocks.plain: Just-you agents show only for you. Approved agents show for everyone.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: You test the agent version you want people to use.

flow.label: Pick version
flow.plain: You choose the active version, or always use the latest.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: Foundry checks your details, builds the app package, and submits it to the catalogs.

flow.label: Choose who
flow.plain: Just you works at once. Organization scope waits for admin approval.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: New versions can roll out through the same address without publishing again.

example.input: Fabrikam finishes testing a support agent in Foundry and wants staff to use it in Teams.
example.output: The team publishes it for the organization. After an admin approves it, staff can find the agent in Microsoft Copilot and Teams.

whenToUse: A tested Foundry agent is ready for people in Teams or Microsoft Copilot.
You want new versions to reach users without publishing again.
whenNot: The portal cannot publish when the project turns off public network access.
Check data flows first. Microsoft 365 and Teams store some publishing data.
fdy-publish-agent-copilot-teams.dataNote: Microsoft 365 and Teams process and store some data from publishing and from the agent's replies. Check that this fits your compliance and data residency rules.

learn.title: Publish agents to Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft Teams in the Foundry portal

fdy-troubleshoot-publishing.definition: Publishing problems fall into three groups: details that fail checks, agents missing from the store, and agents that fail after people start chatting.

blocks.label: Validation
blocks.plain: The version, name, description, and links must meet set rules.

blocks.label: Store search
blocks.plain: Scope and approval decide where an agent appears. The store refreshes about hourly.

blocks.label: After publish
blocks.plain: An agent can work in testing but fail once it is published.

blocks.label: Reset
blocks.plain: A stuck conversation is fixed by starting a new one.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: The publish check names the field that failed.

flow.label: Fix
flow.plain: You correct that field and try again.

flow.label: Find
flow.plain: You check the scope, the approval status, and the store refresh.

flow.label: Check access
flow.plain: If it fails after publishing, you check the agent's permissions on Azure resources.

flow.label: Reset
flow.plain: For a stuck chat, you start a new conversation.

example.input: A Contoso agent works in the Foundry playground but fails in Teams.
example.output: A likely cause is that the agent's identity lacks permission on an Azure resource it uses. Assigning the needed roles fixes it.

whenToUse: Publishing fails with a message about a field.
The agent is missing from the store.
The agent fails after people start using it.
whenNot: A reset conversation cannot be restored.
Guest users cannot use agents in projects with public network access off.

learn.title: Troubleshoot publishing agents to Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft Teams

fdy-evaluate-agent.definition: A Foundry evaluation runs an agent on test data and scores the results with checks called evaluators.

blocks.label: Test data
blocks.plain: A dataset, made-up scenarios, or real conversations to score.

blocks.label: Evaluators
blocks.plain: Agent, quality, and safety checks that each give a score.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.plain: Score single turns, or whole conversations (preview).

blocks.label: Results
blocks.plain: Scores for the whole run and for each result.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: You pick what to score and which test data to use.

flow.label: Pick checks
flow.plain: You pick agent, quality, and safety evaluators.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: Foundry runs the agent on the test data and scores the outputs.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: You read overall scores and individual results.

flow.label: Compare
flow.plain: You compare versions and find repeated failures.

example.input: A Fabrikam team wants to know if its Foundry agent picks the right tool.
example.output: The team runs an evaluation on a test dataset with an agent evaluator, then reads the score for each test question.

whenToUse: You want scores before an agent goes live.
You want to check quality on real conversations.
whenNot: Scoring whole conversations is still in preview.
You need the right project role to run an evaluation.

learn.title: Evaluation in Microsoft Foundry
Run evaluations from the Microsoft Foundry portal

fdy-trace-agent.definition: Tracing records, in order, what a Foundry agent did for each request, so you can find and fix problems.

blocks.label: Application Insights
blocks.plain: The Azure service where Foundry stores traces.

blocks.label: Server-side traces
blocks.plain: Foundry records traces for hosted agents with no code changes.

blocks.label: Conversation view
blocks.plain: Shows history, tokens, run steps, and tool calls for one conversation.

blocks.label: Retention
blocks.plain: The portal shows ready-made traces from the past 90 days.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: A project is connected to an Application Insights resource.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The agent runs, and Foundry logs traces on its own.

flow.label: Search
flow.plain: You search or filter traces from the last 90 days.

flow.label: Step through
flow.plain: You open a trace and look at each part of the work.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: You read the conversation, the tool calls, and the tokens.

example.input: A Contoso agent answers slowly for one customer.
example.output: The team finds the trace for that conversation and sees which tool call or step took the time.

whenToUse: You need to debug a slow or wrong agent run.
You want to watch agent behavior in production.
whenNot: Do not put secrets in prompts or tool arguments, because traces can capture them.
Tracing for workflow agents is still in preview.
fdy-trace-agent.dataNote: Traces can capture user inputs, model outputs, and tool details. Retention and billing follow your Application Insights setup.

learn.title: Set up tracing in Microsoft Foundry

fdy-monitor-agent-dashboard.definition: The dashboard shows how a Foundry agent runs in production: token use, delay, success rate, and scores.

blocks.label: Token usage
blocks.plain: How many tokens the agent traffic used.

blocks.label: Latency
blocks.plain: How long runs take. Over 10 seconds can signal a problem.

blocks.label: Run success rate
blocks.plain: The share of runs that finish. Under 95 percent needs a look.

blocks.label: Evaluations
blocks.plain: Scores from checks that run on sampled outputs.

blocks.label: Settings
blocks.plain: Recurring evaluations, red team scans, and alerts, some in preview.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: Application Insights is connected to the project.

flow.label: Collect
flow.plain: Agent traffic sends data to that resource.

flow.label: View
flow.plain: You pick a time range and read the summary cards and charts.

flow.label: Investigate
flow.plain: You look into failed runs or slow replies.

flow.label: Automate
flow.plain: You add recurring evaluations or alerts.

example.input: Fabrikam notices that agent replies feel slower this week.
example.output: The dashboard shows delay over time, token use, and run success rate for the chosen period, which helps the team decide where to look.

whenToUse: You want a quick view of an agent's health in production.
You want alerts when quality or speed changes.
whenNot: Charts stay empty until the agent has recent traffic.
Red team scans and alerts are in preview.
fdy-monitor-agent-dashboard.dataNote: Monitoring data is stored in your Application Insights resource. Its setup sets how long data stays and what it costs.

learn.title: Monitor agents with the Agent Monitoring Dashboard

fdy-configure-guardrails.definition: A guardrail is a set of safety controls for Foundry models and agents, and each control names a risk, where to check, and what to do.

blocks.label: Risk
blocks.plain: The kind of harm to watch for, such as violence or hate.

blocks.label: Check point
blocks.plain: Where to check, such as the user input or the output.

blocks.label: Action
blocks.plain: What happens when the risk is found.

blocks.label: Assignment
blocks.plain: A guardrail is assigned to models and agents.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: You create a guardrail and add controls.

flow.label: Add controls
flow.plain: Each control sets a risk, check points, and one action.

flow.label: Assign
flow.plain: You assign the guardrail to models and agents.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: You test it in the playground before production.

flow.label: Adjust
flow.plain: You edit or override controls as needed.

example.input: A Contoso team wants its Foundry agent to block violent content in user input and output.
example.output: The team adds controls for the violence risk at the input and output points, assigns the guardrail to the agent, and tests it.

whenToUse: You want safety checks on a model or agent.
You want to test guardrail behavior before production.
whenNot: Microsoft default guardrails cannot be edited. Make a custom one.
Some controls can only be overridden, not deleted.

learn.title: How to configure guardrails and controls in Microsoft Foundry

fdy-foundry-rbac.definition: Foundry roles give people only the access they need, at the right scope, when they sign in with Microsoft Entra ID.

blocks.label: Role
blocks.plain: A named group of permissions, such as Foundry User.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.plain: Where a role applies: the resource, a project, or one agent.

blocks.label: Agent Consumer
blocks.plain: A least-privilege role for people who only chat with agents.

blocks.label: Key sign-in
blocks.plain: Keys give full access with no role limits.

flow.label: List people
flow.plain: You sort people into builders, managers, and agent users.

flow.label: Pick roles
flow.plain: You match each person to the least-privilege role.

flow.label: Pick scope
flow.plain: You assign it at the right level, down to a single agent.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: You check that access works as planned.

example.input: Fabrikam wants support staff to chat with a Foundry agent but not change it.
example.output: The team gives them the Foundry Agent Consumer role, which lets them interact with agents and nothing more.

whenToUse: You need different access for builders and agent users.
You want to grant access to one agent only.
whenNot: Key-based sign-in skips roles and gives full access.
The Azure AI Developer role is not for Foundry projects.

learn.title: Role-based access control for Microsoft Foundry
