fdy-manage-costs.definition: Foundry cost tools help you estimate, track, and limit what AI workloads cost, using the same data that finance teams see.

blocks.label: Plan
blocks.plain: Estimate costs before you deploy with the Azure pricing calculator.

blocks.label: Track
blocks.plain: See cost by subscription, project, agent, and model deployment.

blocks.label: Control
blocks.plain: Budgets send alerts. Cost controls (preview) can also block requests.

blocks.label: Delay
blocks.plain: Usage shows in minutes. Cost appears 8 to 24 hours later.

flow.label: Estimate
flow.plain: A team estimates costs with the Azure pricing calculator.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: Agents and models run, and usage shows up within minutes.

flow.label: Bill
flow.plain: Cost data arrives 8 to 24 hours after the usage.

flow.label: Track
flow.plain: Teams see costs by project, agent, and model deployment.

flow.label: Control
flow.plain: Budgets alert. Preview cost controls can alert or block requests.

example.input: Contoso wants to know what one Foundry agent costs each month.
example.output: The team checks the project and agent cost pages, which use Azure Cost Management data, and sets a budget alert for the month.

whenToUse: You need to know what a project or agent costs.
You want an alert before spending runs over.
whenNot: Current-month cost is an estimate until the invoice is final.
Azure budgets alert but do not block requests.

learn.title: Cost and FinOps in Microsoft Foundry

dca-agent-builder-share-agent.definition: Sharing gives chosen people direct access to an Agent Builder agent, as owners who can edit or as chat users who can only talk to it.

blocks.label: Can edit
blocks.plain: Owners can edit, share, and manage the agent.

blocks.label: Can chat
blocks.plain: Chat users can only talk to the agent.

blocks.label: Update
blocks.plain: Changes save on their own but reach users after an update.

blocks.label: Admin limits
blocks.plain: Admins can limit who may share with the whole organization.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: A new agent starts private to its creator.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: The owner adds people or groups, or copies a link.

flow.label: Chat
flow.plain: Chat users talk to the agent, which respects each person's access.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: The owner updates the agent, and changes can take several minutes to appear.

example.input: A Contoso team lead builds a policy helper agent and wants her team to try it.
example.output: She shares it with her team as chat users. They can ask questions, and they only get content they are allowed to see.

whenToUse: You are piloting an agent with a known group.
You want teammates to co-own and edit an agent.
whenNot: Sharing does not publish the agent across the organization or other channels.
A group can only be a chat user, never an owner.
dca-agent-builder-share-agent.dataNote: The agent follows each person's own permissions and labels. Someone without access to a source gets answers without that content.

learn.title: Share and manage agents built in Agent Builder

dca-agent-builder-share-and-catalog.definition: Submitting to the company catalog asks an admin to review an agent and add it to the Agent Store.

blocks.label: Shared version
blocks.plain: What you update. Changes reach shared users right away.

blocks.label: Store version
blocks.plain: The listing an admin manages. It changes only after approval.

blocks.label: Admin review
blocks.plain: Admins check the name, capabilities, knowledge sources, and label.

blocks.label: Status
blocks.plain: Waiting, approved, or rejected with the reviewer's comment.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: You publish the agent at least once.

flow.label: Submit
flow.plain: You fill in the display details and submit.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: An admin reviews the agent and approves or rejects it.

flow.label: List
flow.plain: If approved, it appears in the store as built by your organization.

flow.label: Resubmit
flow.plain: Later updates need a new submission and a new approval.

example.input: A Fabrikam team wants its tested agent available to the whole company.
example.output: The team submits it for admin review. After approval, the people the admin allows can find it in the store.

whenToUse: The agent is production-ready and needs broad availability.
You want an admin to review it before wide use.
whenNot: Updates do not reach the store until an admin approves a resubmission.
Only one submission can be pending at a time.

learn.title: Submit agents from Agent Builder to your org catalog

dca-toolkit-developer-mode.definition: Developer mode shows a debug card that tells you what Copilot's orchestrator used to answer a message.

blocks.label: Debug card
blocks.plain: Appears when the orchestrator searches knowledge or uses actions.

blocks.label: Capabilities
blocks.plain: Whether each capability was used, with a downloadable log.

blocks.label: Actions
blocks.plain: Which functions matched the prompt, and which were selected.

blocks.label: Local preview
blocks.plain: A test of the agent in a browser-based Copilot Chat.

flow.label: Preview
flow.plain: You start the agent in a browser-based Copilot Chat.

flow.label: Switch on
flow.plain: You switch developer mode on in the chat.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: You send a prompt, and the orchestrator picks what to use.

flow.label: Read card
flow.plain: A card shows the knowledge, capabilities, and actions it considered.

flow.label: Fix
flow.plain: You fix unclear descriptions or broken actions.

example.input: A developer sends a test question and gets a wrong answer.
example.output: The debug card shows whether the orchestrator found the agent's knowledge or actions, so the developer can see where it went wrong.

whenToUse: You want to know why an action was not chosen.
You want to debug an agent locally before sharing it.
whenNot: No card appears if the orchestrator needs no Microsoft 365 data or skills.
Developer mode works only in the licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot experience.

learn.title: Use developer mode to test and debug agents in Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit

dca-agent-builder-troubleshooting.definition: When an Agent Builder agent cannot be shared or updated, the message points to the cause, such as harmful content or an unsupported label.

blocks.label: Safety check
blocks.plain: Agents that might encourage harmful actions cannot be updated.

blocks.label: Labels
blocks.plain: Files with unsupported labels stop the agent from being created.

blocks.label: Policy changes
blocks.plain: If sharing no longer fits admin policy, fix it before updating.

blocks.label: Sharing errors
blocks.plain: A failed share can leave people without access to knowledge files.

flow.label: Try
flow.plain: An owner creates, shares, or updates an agent.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The product checks content, labels, and sharing rules.

flow.label: Message
flow.plain: If a check fails, a message names the problem.

flow.label: Fix
flow.plain: The owner edits the details, files, or sharing settings.

flow.label: Retry
flow.plain: The owner tries again.

example.input: A Contoso maker cannot update an agent.
example.output: The message says the agent might encourage harmful actions. The maker removes the harmful content and tries again.

whenToUse: An update or a share fails and you need to know why.
An uploaded file is rejected.
whenNot: Fixing file access may need the file owner or a site admin.
Some errors are service errors. Wait a few minutes or contact support.

learn.title: Share and manage agents built in Agent Builder

dca-admin-agent-settings.definition: The agent settings page lets admins decide which kinds of agents people can use, who may share them, who can use them, and whether feedback is shared.

blocks.label: Agent types
blocks.plain: Allow agents from Microsoft, your own teams, or outside publishers.

blocks.label: Sharing
blocks.plain: All users, no users, or specific users may share org-wide.

blocks.label: User access
blocks.plain: All users, no users, or specific users or groups may use agents.

blocks.label: Feedback
blocks.plain: Decides whether developers get ratings and comments.

blocks.label: Rules and tags
blocks.plain: Management rules, templates, and tags keep agents organized.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: An admin decides who may build, share, and use agents.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: The settings apply to the whole organization.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: Sharing limits cover only agents built with Agent Builder.

flow.label: Notice
flow.plain: Changes to sharing apply to new sharing actions, not old ones.

example.input: Contoso wants only a few people to share agents across the company.
example.output: An admin limits org-wide sharing to specific users or groups. Agents already shared stay available unless owners change them.

whenToUse: You need to control who can install or use agents.
You want to manage how sharing works across the organization.
whenNot: The sharing control covers only Agent Builder agents.
Microsoft's terms do not cover data handled by other companies.

learn.title: Agent settings in Microsoft 365 admin center

dca-admin-agent-registry.definition: The agent registry lists the company's agents so admins can see owners, find ownerless ones, and block or delete them.

blocks.label: Registry
blocks.plain: A central list of agents, with filters by publisher type.

blocks.label: Publisher types
blocks.plain: Microsoft, external partner, published by your org, or shared by creator.

blocks.label: No owner
blocks.plain: Shared agents become ownerless when their creator is deleted.

blocks.label: Actions
blocks.plain: Admins can block or delete an agent, or change its owner.

flow.label: List
flow.plain: Admins open the registry and see every agent.

flow.label: Filter
flow.plain: They filter by publisher type, owner, or other details.

flow.label: Spot
flow.plain: A card counts agents that no longer have an owner.

flow.label: Act
flow.plain: They block or delete those agents, or give them a new owner.

example.input: A Contoso employee who built several shared agents leaves the company.
example.output: Those shared agents become ownerless. An admin finds them in the registry and blocks, deletes, or reassigns them.

whenToUse: You need to see which agents exist and who owns them.
You want to clean up agents that nobody owns.
whenNot: The same agent can appear in more than one row. This is by design.
Groups cannot own agents built in Agent Builder.

learn.title: Manage agent registry in Microsoft 365 admin center

dca-licensing-and-environment.definition: Which agent features people can use depends on their license or on usage-based billing, so check early.

blocks.label: Copilot license
blocks.plain: Full agent features, including agents grounded in tenant data.

blocks.label: Usage-based billing
blocks.plain: Lets people use agents without a full license, measured in Copilot Credits.

blocks.label: No license
blocks.plain: Agent access is limited or turned off.

blocks.label: Dev environment
blocks.plain: A sandbox, a licensed work tenant, or a basic tenant for testing.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: You list the capabilities your agent needs.

flow.label: Match
flow.plain: You match them to the licensing models in your tenant.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: You pick a development environment that supports them.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: You confirm that a test user has the license the agent needs.

example.input: A Fabrikam team wants an agent grounded in SharePoint data, but most users lack a Copilot license.
example.output: The team enables usage-based billing for the tenant, so people can use the agent without a full license. Usage is measured in Copilot Credits.

whenToUse: You are planning which agent features your tenant can use.
You need to choose a development environment.
whenNot: Usage-based billing is not supported in the government clouds.
Email, people, and Teams knowledge need a Microsoft 365 Copilot license.

learn.title: Set up your development environment for your plugin

m365h-assign-copilot-licenses.definition: Microsoft Copilot is an add-on for eligible plans, and an admin gives each person a license.

blocks.label: Eligible plan
blocks.plain: A prerequisite license that qualifies people for the add-on.

blocks.label: Add-on
blocks.plain: The Microsoft Copilot license bought on top of a plan.

blocks.label: Business option
blocks.plain: Copilot Business fits companies with up to 300 users.

blocks.label: Assignment
blocks.plain: Admins assign licenses to users.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: An admin checks that the organization's plans are eligible.

flow.label: Buy
flow.plain: The organization buys Copilot licenses.

flow.label: Assign
flow.plain: An admin assigns each license to a user.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: A diagnostic tool can check a person's access.

example.input: Contoso buys Copilot licenses for its finance team.
example.output: An admin assigns the licenses to the finance users. People with a license can use agents grounded in tenant data.

whenToUse: People need Copilot features in Microsoft 365 apps.
You need to confirm that a plan is eligible before buying.
whenNot: Licensing terms can change, so confirm eligibility before you buy.
Copilot Business supports up to 300 licensed users per tenant.

learn.title: License options for Microsoft Copilot

m365h-measure-copilot-adoption.definition: Copilot reports show how many people have a license, how many use it, and how often, so you can see where adoption lags.

blocks.label: Enabled users
blocks.plain: People who have a Copilot license.

blocks.label: Active users
blocks.plain: Licensed people who tried a Copilot feature.

blocks.label: Active rate
blocks.plain: Active users divided by enabled users.

blocks.label: Dashboard
blocks.plain: The Copilot Dashboard adds readiness, adoption, and impact.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: People use Copilot in their apps.

flow.label: Report
flow.plain: A day's activity typically shows in the usage report within 48 hours.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: Admins read enabled users, active users, and the active rate.

flow.label: Trend
flow.plain: They view trends over 7, 28, 90, or 180 days.

flow.label: Explore
flow.plain: They use the Copilot Dashboard to look at readiness, adoption, and impact.

example.input: A Contoso IT lead wants to know if people with Copilot licenses really use it.
example.output: The usage report shows enabled users, active users, and the active users rate, with trends over time.

whenToUse: You need to see how many licensed people use Copilot.
You want trends over weeks or months.
whenNot: A day's data typically appears only after about 48 hours.
Use agent monitoring to see how one agent performs.

learn.title: Microsoft Copilot usage report

m365h-secure-copilot-data.definition: The Copilot security blueprint has three parts: fix oversharing, set guardrails, and meet AI rules.

blocks.label: Fix oversharing
blocks.plain: Find content that too many people can reach, and tighten access.

blocks.label: Guardrails
blocks.plain: Enforceable safeguards that protect Copilot interactions.

blocks.label: Regulations
blocks.plain: Close gaps in AI rules, audit needs, and data hygiene.

blocks.label: Tools
blocks.plain: Microsoft Purview and SharePoint Advanced Management support the work.

flow.label: Find
flow.plain: Admins identify high-risk sites and files.

flow.label: Limit
flow.plain: They apply interim access limits if needed.

flow.label: Fix
flow.plain: They fix the access issues for good.

flow.label: Enforce
flow.plain: They keep guardrails in place over time.

example.input: Contoso plans a Copilot rollout and worries that old sites are shared too widely.
example.output: The team finds high-risk sites, limits access for now, fixes permissions, and then turns on lasting guardrails.

whenToUse: You are preparing for a Copilot rollout.
You want a simple order of steps for securing data.
whenNot: The blueprint is a plan to follow, not a single setting.
Specific roles and tools vary by task. Check each linked guide.

learn.title: Secure and govern Microsoft Copilot: Foundational deployment guidance

m365h-review-agent-inventory.definition: The agent overview and registry show admins which agents exist, who owns them, and which need attention.

blocks.label: Registry
blocks.plain: A central list of agents that admins can filter.

blocks.label: Publisher types
blocks.plain: Microsoft, external partner, published by your org, or shared by creator.

blocks.label: Overview cards
blocks.plain: Counts, such as agents that have no owner.

blocks.label: Duplicate rows
blocks.plain: One agent can show in several rows by design.

flow.label: Open
flow.plain: Admins open the overview and the registry.

flow.label: Filter
flow.plain: They filter by publisher type, owner, or state.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: They look for agents that need attention, such as ownerless ones.

flow.label: Act
flow.plain: They block, delete, or reassign those agents.

example.input: A Fabrikam admin wants to see every agent that employees have shared.
example.output: The registry lists agents shared by their creators, with owners and status, so the admin can follow up on any that need care.

whenToUse: You need an organization-wide list of agents.
You want to find agents that need attention.
whenNot: The same Copilot Studio agent can appear twice with different publisher types.
The registry also lists agents built by Microsoft and outside partners.

learn.title: Manage agent registry in Microsoft 365 admin center

m365h-control-agent-availability.definition: Admins decide which agent types people can install, who can use agents, and who gets an approved agent.

blocks.label: Agent types
blocks.plain: Allow agents from Microsoft, your own teams, or outside publishers.

blocks.label: User access
blocks.plain: All users, no users, or specific users or groups.

blocks.label: Sharing
blocks.plain: Who may share Agent Builder agents with the organization.

blocks.label: Audience
blocks.plain: Publishing picks who can install an agent and who gets it preinstalled.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: An admin decides which agent types and users are allowed.

flow.label: Set
flow.plain: The settings apply across the organization.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: For a requested agent, the admin picks the audience.

flow.label: Adjust
flow.plain: The admin can change access as needs change.

example.input: Contoso wants only approved agents from its own teams to be installable.
example.output: An admin allows agents built by the organization and turns off agents from outside publishers.

whenToUse: You need to control which agents people can find and install.
You want to pick the audience for an approved agent.
whenNot: The sharing control covers only Agent Builder agents.
Review non-Microsoft publishers' terms before allowing their agents.

learn.title: Agent settings in Microsoft 365 admin center
Manage agent requests in Microsoft 365 admin center

m365h-approve-agent-requests.definition: An admin reviews each agent sent in for the company, picks a policy template, and then publishes or rejects it.

blocks.label: Requests list
blocks.plain: Shows agents waiting for review, update, or activation.

blocks.label: Review
blocks.plain: Admins check what the agent can do and what it can reach.

blocks.label: Policy template
blocks.plain: A bundle of policies from Entra, Purview, SharePoint, and Defender.

blocks.label: Decision
blocks.plain: Publish to the store for chosen users, or reject.

flow.label: Submit
flow.plain: A maker submits an agent for the organization.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: An admin reads the agent's details and permissions.

flow.label: Template
flow.plain: The admin picks a policy template for the agent.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The admin publishes it to chosen users or rejects it.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: Later updates wait for approval, so users keep the old version.

example.input: A Fabrikam maker submits a new agent built in Copilot Studio.
example.output: An admin reviews the agent's data and tools, applies a template, and publishes it to the chosen users.

whenToUse: You need a review step before agents reach the organization.
You want security policies applied to each new agent.
whenNot: Template changes apply to new activations, not agents already approved.
Custom templates need an Agent 365 license.

learn.title: Manage agent requests in Microsoft 365 admin center
Policy templates

ppai-human-review-prompt-output.definition: Human review adds a person to an automated flow, so text from a prompt is approved before the flow uses it.

blocks.label: Prompt output
blocks.plain: Text that a generative AI model writes inside a flow.

blocks.label: Approval
blocks.plain: A person approves or rejects that text.

blocks.label: Outcome check
blocks.plain: The flow continues based on the approval result.

blocks.label: Risks
blocks.plain: Models can invent facts, and hidden instructions can mislead them.

flow.label: Generate
flow.plain: A prompt in a flow writes some text.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: The flow sends the text to a person for approval.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The person approves or rejects it.

flow.label: Continue
flow.plain: The flow uses the text only if it was approved.

example.input: A flow drafts replies to customer complaints.
example.output: A person reads each draft and approves it before it is sent, which helps catch made-up or injected content.

whenToUse: A flow sends AI-written text to customers.
A mistake in the text would be costly.
whenNot: Filters alone do not remove made-up or injected content.
It slows the flow, because a person must respond.

learn.title: Human review for automation with a prompt

ppai-admin-governance-security.definition: AI Builder governance lets admins turn AI prompts and preview models on or off per environment, and control who can create, use, and share models.

blocks.label: Feature switches
blocks.plain: AI prompts and preview models can be turned off per environment.

blocks.label: Data policies
blocks.plain: AI Builder is part of the Dataverse connector in data policies.

blocks.label: Roles
blocks.plain: Makers create, basic users use shared items, and admins see all.

blocks.label: Sharing
blocks.plain: A model or prompt is private to its owner until shared.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: An admin decides which AI features each environment gets.

flow.label: Set roles
flow.plain: Security roles decide who can create and who can use.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: Owners share models and prompts with other users.

flow.label: Enforce
flow.plain: Data policies stop blocked connectors from being used.

example.input: Contoso wants makers to try AI prompts but not preview models.
example.output: An admin keeps AI prompts on and turns off the preview and experimental models setting for that environment.

whenToUse: You need to control AI features by environment.
You need makers and users to have different access.
whenNot: Turning a feature off breaks flows and apps that already use it.
Business and non-business connectors cannot share data in one flow.

learn.title: Administer AI Builder
Roles and security in AI Builder

ppai-alm-distribute-models.definition: An AI model moves between environments inside a solution that you export and then import.

blocks.label: Published version
blocks.plain: Only a published version can go into a solution.

blocks.label: Solution
blocks.plain: The package that carries the model between environments.

blocks.label: Not included
blocks.plain: Training data stays behind. Only the model itself moves.

blocks.label: Dependencies
blocks.plain: Apps and flows that use the model must be added too.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The model gets a published version.

flow.label: Package
flow.plain: The model is added to a solution.

flow.label: Export
flow.plain: The solution is exported as a file.

flow.label: Import
flow.plain: The solution is imported in the target environment.

flow.label: Protect
flow.plain: Customizing can be turned off to keep the model from being changed.

example.input: Fabrikam builds a model in a test environment and needs it in production.
example.output: The team packages the published model in a solution, exports it, and imports it as managed in production, where it can be used at once.

whenToUse: You develop models in one environment and use them in another.
You want to automate how models move between environments.
whenNot: Some imported model types cannot be retrained, because training data stays behind.
A model is not counted as an app or flow dependency.

learn.title: Distribute your model using a solution

ppai-credits-licensing-transition.definition: Running AI Builder models and prompts uses AI Builder credits or Copilot Credits, and admins allocate and watch them to avoid capacity errors.

blocks.label: Free to try
blocks.plain: Building and testing models and prompts does not use credits.

blocks.label: Runs use credits
blocks.plain: Running them in flows and apps uses credits.

blocks.label: Overage
blocks.plain: When AI Builder credits run out, Copilot Credits are tried next.

blocks.label: Transition
blocks.plain: New customers buy Copilot Credits, not AI Builder credits.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: Building and testing does not use credits.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: Running a model in a flow or app uses credits.

flow.label: Overage
flow.plain: If AI Builder credits run out, the system tries Copilot Credits.

flow.label: Block
flow.plain: If neither is available, runs fail with capacity errors.

flow.label: Fix
flow.plain: Admins move credits around or add Copilot Credits.

example.input: A Contoso flow that uses an AI Builder prompt suddenly fails.
example.output: The environment may be out of credits. An admin moves credits or adds Copilot Credits so the flow can run again.

whenToUse: You plan credits for AI Builder in an environment.
You see capacity errors in a flow or app.
whenNot: Usage is counted only from time to time, sometimes days apart.
AI Builder credits are being phased out in favor of Copilot Credits.

learn.title: Licensing and AI Builder credits

ppai-monitor-ai-activity.definition: The AI Builder activity page lists runs of AI models and prompts from flows, apps, and Copilot Studio, and admins can export and clean up that data.

blocks.label: Activity list
blocks.plain: Shows time, tool name, input, output, and consumption.

blocks.label: Sources
blocks.plain: Power Automate, Power Apps, and Copilot Studio.

blocks.label: Who sees what
blocks.plain: Admins see all activity. Makers and basic users see their own.

blocks.label: Data cleanup
blocks.plain: A scheduled bulk delete keeps the table from growing too large.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: A model or prompt runs in a flow, an app, or an agent.

flow.label: Record
flow.plain: The run is saved in a Dataverse table.

flow.label: View
flow.plain: People see the activity their role allows.

flow.label: Export
flow.plain: The data can be exported to a file.

flow.label: Clean up
flow.plain: A bulk delete job removes old records.

example.input: A Fabrikam admin wants to see which AI models and prompts use the most capacity.
example.output: The activity page lists each run with its source and consumption. The admin can export the data to a file.

whenToUse: You want to see how AI models and prompts are used.
The activity table is growing and needs cleanup.
whenNot: Deleted records cannot be recovered, so test the filter first.
The table holds the input of text scenarios only.
ppai-monitor-ai-activity.dataNote: Activity data is stored in a Dataverse table and stays even if the model, flow, or app is deleted. It holds the input for text scenarios only.

learn.title: Monitor AI Builder models and prompts activity

spai-share-agent-and-manage-access.definition: Sharing an agent that uses SharePoint content gives people direct access, but the agent shows only what each person can see.

blocks.label: Can edit
blocks.plain: Owners edit, share, and manage the agent.

blocks.label: Can chat
blocks.plain: Chat users only talk to the agent.

blocks.label: Knowledge sharing
blocks.plain: Owners can also share chosen SharePoint files and folders.

blocks.label: Site access
blocks.plain: Full site access is not shared. A site admin must grant it.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: The owner adds owners and chat users.

flow.label: Share files
flow.plain: Chosen SharePoint files and folders can be shared with them.

flow.label: Chat
flow.plain: Each person gets answers based on what they can access.

flow.label: Fix
flow.plain: If sharing fails, the owner asks the file owner or site admin for access.

example.input: A Contoso owner shares a policy agent with a team, but one teammate cannot open one of its SharePoint sites.
example.output: That teammate can still chat with the agent, but the answers leave out content from the site they cannot access.

whenToUse: You want a team to try an agent grounded in SharePoint content.
You want co-owners who can edit the agent.
whenNot: Sharing the agent does not publish it to other channels.
Removing someone's agent access does not remove their file access.

learn.title: Share and manage agents built in Agent Builder

spai-sam-overview-and-licensing.definition: SharePoint Advanced Management is a toolset that helps admins tidy, track, and protect content in SharePoint and OneDrive.

blocks.label: Content sprawl
blocks.plain: Find and reduce unneeded or unmanaged content.

blocks.label: Content lifecycle
blocks.plain: Track changes and group sites in categories.

blocks.label: Oversharing
blocks.plain: Reports, reviews, and limits on who can reach content.

blocks.label: Prerequisites
blocks.plain: Licenses and roles are listed on a separate page.

flow.label: Assess
flow.plain: Admins assess how content is shared and kept.

flow.label: Reduce
flow.plain: They reduce unneeded or unowned content.

flow.label: Limit
flow.plain: They limit access with reports, reviews, and policies.

flow.label: Repeat
flow.plain: They repeat the checks as content changes.

example.input: Contoso wants cleaner SharePoint content before a Copilot rollout.
example.output: Admins use these reports to find inactive, ownerless, or overshared sites, then act on the findings.

whenToUse: You want to tidy SharePoint and OneDrive content.
You want to prevent oversharing before a Copilot rollout.
whenNot: Some controls need extra licenses. Check the prerequisites first.
It is built for SharePoint and Microsoft 365 admins.

learn.title: What is SharePoint Advanced Management?

spai-copilot-credits-advanced-work.definition: Copilot in SharePoint is a mix: everyday work comes with the Microsoft 365 Copilot license, and advanced work uses Copilot Credits.

blocks.label: Everyday work
blocks.plain: Questions, drafting, and organizing come with the license.

blocks.label: Advanced work
blocks.plain: Work at scale, such as whole sites, uses Copilot Credits.

blocks.label: Spending policy
blocks.plain: An admin sets who may use credits, with limits and alerts.

blocks.label: Who needs credits
blocks.plain: Content and site managers first. Most others likely do not.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks Copilot in SharePoint for help.

flow.label: Everyday
flow.plain: Everyday tasks are covered by the license.

flow.label: Confirm
flow.plain: For advanced work, a person with credits is asked to confirm.

flow.label: Track
flow.plain: Users can check how many credits a task used.

flow.label: Warn
flow.plain: Users are warned when 20 percent of the monthly limit remains.

example.input: A Fabrikam site manager asks Copilot to build a whole site and process a large set of documents.
example.output: That is advanced work. The manager confirms the credit use first, and the admin's spending policy sets the limits.

whenToUse: People manage sites and content at scale.
You need a spending limit for advanced work.
whenNot: Everyday use does not need credits.
Credit use varies with task type, complexity, and content volume.

learn.title: Get started with Copilot in SharePoint

spai-upgrade-agent-files.definition: The old .agent file format is being retired, so each agent should move to a new path that fits what it does.

blocks.label: Site questions
blocks.plain: Use Copilot in SharePoint directly.

blocks.label: Repeatable task
blocks.plain: Turn the agent into a skill.

blocks.label: Custom Q&A
blocks.plain: Rebuild it with Agent Builder.

blocks.label: Copilot Studio agent
blocks.plain: Publish it to the Microsoft Copilot app instead.

flow.label: List
flow.plain: You list your existing agent files.

flow.label: Match
flow.plain: You match each agent to the path that fits its job.

flow.label: Upgrade
flow.plain: You rebuild or convert it on that path.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: You share it, and admins manage it centrally.

example.input: Contoso has an agent file that answers questions about its HR policy library.
example.output: Because it gives a customized Q&A experience, the team upgrades it with Agent Builder and shares it again.

whenToUse: You have agents saved as .agent files.
You want your agents managed with central admin tools.
whenNot: Only the file format is retiring, not agents in SharePoint.
Existing files keep working for a while, so plan the upgrade.

learn.title: Upgrade agents in SharePoint and OneDrive

spai-content-management-assessment.definition: The content management assessment runs a set of reports and lists what to fix before a Copilot rollout.

blocks.label: Reports
blocks.plain: Inactive sites, ownership, broken inheritance, and risky sharing.

blocks.label: Dashboard
blocks.plain: Shows affected sites, findings, and recommended actions.

blocks.label: No auto action
blocks.plain: The reports take no action without the admin's consent.

blocks.label: Rerun
blocks.plain: Run again about every 30 days to track progress.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: An admin starts the assessment.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: It runs the reports, which can take from 2 to 72 hours.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: The admin reviews impacted sites and findings.

flow.label: Act
flow.plain: The admin follows the recommended steps.

flow.label: Repeat
flow.plain: The admin reruns it about every 30 days.

example.input: Fabrikam wants to know how ready its SharePoint content is for Copilot.
example.output: The dashboard flags inactive sites, ownerless sites, and broad sharing, with suggested next steps for each.

whenToUse: You are preparing for a Copilot rollout.
You do not know where to start with governance.
whenNot: Reports can take hours to run, depending on tenant size.
The assessment finds issues. It does not fix them for you.

learn.title: Assess your organization's content management status

spai-restricted-content-discovery.definition: Restricted Content Discovery hides a site from search and Copilot answers while its access is checked.

blocks.label: Site setting
blocks.plain: A setting on one SharePoint site.

blocks.label: Permissions
blocks.plain: They stay the same. People who have access keep it.

blocks.label: Search index
blocks.plain: Content stays in the index, so Purview tools still work.

blocks.label: Temporary
blocks.plain: Meant as a short-term control, used selectively.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: An admin picks sites that need review.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: The setting is applied, and it takes time to spread.

flow.label: Hide
flow.plain: The site's content stops showing in company-wide search and Copilot.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: Owners review and fix permissions.

flow.label: Remove
flow.plain: The admin removes the setting when the review is done.

example.input: Contoso is reviewing permissions on its finance sites before a Copilot rollout.
example.output: An admin restricts discovery for those sites. Their content stops appearing in company-wide search and Copilot while owners clean up access.

whenToUse: A site has a high risk of oversharing.
A phased Copilot rollout needs time to review sites.
whenNot: It does not change permissions, so direct access still works.
Too much use can make search and AI answers less complete.
It covers SharePoint sites only, not OneDrive.
spai-restricted-content-discovery.dataNote: It does not remove content from the search index, and Microsoft Purview tools such as eDiscovery keep working.

learn.title: Restrict discovery of SharePoint sites and content

spai-restricted-access-control.definition: Restricted access control limits a site to members of chosen groups, so others cannot open it or see it in search or Copilot.

blocks.label: Control groups
blocks.plain: Up to 10 Microsoft 365 or Entra security groups per site.

blocks.label: Two checks
blocks.plain: A person needs site permission and membership in a control group.

blocks.label: Search and Copilot
blocks.plain: They honor the policy, so outsiders see nothing.

blocks.label: Channel sites
blocks.plain: Shared and private channel sites need their own setup.

flow.label: Allow
flow.plain: An admin allows the policy across the company.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: Groups are chosen for a site.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: People outside the groups lose access, even with a link.

flow.label: Wait
flow.plain: Search and Copilot take time to reflect the change.

example.input: Fabrikam wants a legal site open only to the legal team.
example.output: An admin sets the legal group as the control group. Others cannot open the site, and its content stays out of their search and Copilot.

whenToUse: A site must be limited to a known group.
You want search and Copilot to honor that limit.
whenNot: Adding someone to the group does not give them site access.
Larger sites take longer to reflect the policy.

learn.title: Restrict SharePoint site access with Microsoft 365 groups and Microsoft Entra security groups

spai-site-access-review.definition: Site access reviews let admins ask site owners to check who can reach a site, using reports that flag oversharing.

blocks.label: Access reports
blocks.plain: Snapshot and activity reports that show where sharing is wide.

blocks.label: Access review
blocks.plain: A request for a site owner to check who has access.

blocks.label: Owners
blocks.plain: Site owners complete the review.

blocks.label: AI insights
blocks.plain: AI suggests patterns and next steps from a report.

flow.label: Report
flow.plain: An admin generates a data access governance report.

flow.label: Spot
flow.plain: The report points to sites that may be overshared.

flow.label: Request
flow.plain: The admin starts a site access review.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: Site owners check who has access and fix what is too wide.

example.input: Contoso finds that many sites are shared with everyone except external users.
example.output: An admin starts site access reviews from the report, and site owners check who should still have access.

whenToUse: A report shows sites that may be overshared.
You want owners, not IT, to confirm who needs access.
whenNot: A report alone does not change access.
Sharing link reports cover the last 28 days.

learn.title: What is SharePoint Advanced Management?

spai-site-lifecycle-policies.definition: Site lifecycle policies find sites with no owner or activity, and ask owners to confirm the sites are still needed.

blocks.label: Ownership policy
blocks.plain: Sets who is responsible for each site.

blocks.label: Inactive site policy
blocks.plain: Finds sites with no recent activity and notifies owners.

blocks.label: Attestation
blocks.plain: Asks owners or admins to confirm the site's details.

blocks.label: Enforcement
blocks.plain: Actions taken when there is no response.

flow.label: Define
flow.plain: An admin creates a policy.

flow.label: Detect
flow.plain: The policy checks activity across SharePoint, Teams, Viva Engage, and Exchange.

flow.label: Notify
flow.plain: Owners or admins are told and asked to confirm the site is needed.

flow.label: Enforce
flow.plain: If nobody responds, the policy can take an enforcement action.

example.input: Fabrikam has hundreds of abandoned team sites.
example.output: An inactive site policy notifies each site's owners, asks them to confirm the site is needed, and can act if nobody replies.

whenToUse: Many sites are unused or have no owner.
You want regular owner reviews of sites.
whenNot: OneDrive sites are out of scope for inactive site checks.
Activity through an app token does not count as site activity.

learn.title: Manage inactive sites by using inactive site policies
What is SharePoint Advanced Management?

spai-control-agent-access.definition: To govern agents that use SharePoint content, admins answer three questions: who can use them, what they can reach, and where they are available.

blocks.label: Who
blocks.plain: Copilot licenses, or pay-as-you-go billing for a group.

blocks.label: What
blocks.plain: Agents follow each person's access. Labels and data loss prevention can keep files out.

blocks.label: Where
blocks.plain: Site owners pick a main agent. Restricted content discovery turns agents off.

blocks.label: Block
blocks.plain: Admins can block agents from being used in Copilot Chat.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks an agent a question.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The agent uses only content that person can access.

flow.label: Filter
flow.plain: Labels and policies can keep chosen files out of answers.

flow.label: Place
flow.plain: Site settings decide where the agent shows up.

example.input: Contoso wants a finance site to stay out of agents for now.
example.output: An admin turns on restricted content discovery for the site. Its agent features disappear, and its content stops surfacing in Copilot.

whenToUse: You need to decide who can use agents.
You need to keep chosen content away from agents.
whenNot: The page describes .agent files, which are being upgraded.
Agent access does not widen what people can already see.

learn.title: Manage access to agents in SharePoint

spai-agent-insights-reports.definition: Agent insights reports show which agents exist in SharePoint and OneDrive and how agents reach their content.

blocks.label: Agents in SharePoint
blocks.plain: Shows recently created agents and the sites with the most agents.

blocks.label: Agent access
blocks.plain: Shows how agents interact with SharePoint and OneDrive content.

blocks.label: Reports
blocks.plain: SharePoint admins generate these reports.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: An admin creates an agent insights report.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: The report lists agents and the sites that hold the most.

flow.label: Check access
flow.plain: The access report shows how agents reach site content.

flow.label: Act
flow.plain: Admins use what they learn to tighten access.

example.input: Contoso wants to know how many agents were created on its sites.
example.output: The report lists recently created agents and the sites with the most agents.

whenToUse: You want to see where agents exist in SharePoint.
You want to know how agents reach site content.
whenNot: These reports show agent activity, not whether answers are good.
Check the prerequisites page for the licenses and roles you need.

learn.title: What is SharePoint Advanced Management?

spai-sharepoint-admin-agent.definition: The SharePoint Admin Agent lets admins ask questions in plain language about content risks and get guided help to fix them.

blocks.label: Plain prompts
blocks.plain: Admins ask questions instead of running reports by hand.

blocks.label: Data sources
blocks.plain: It analyzes data from SharePoint and SharePoint Advanced Management.

blocks.label: Topics
blocks.plain: Content sprawl, lifecycle, oversharing, and permissions.

blocks.label: Where
blocks.plain: Available in the Microsoft Copilot app, the SharePoint admin center, and Teams.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: An admin asks a question, such as which sites are overshared.

flow.label: Gather
flow.plain: The agent gathers the relevant data and reports.

flow.label: Advise
flow.plain: It gives analysis and recommendations.

flow.label: Next
flow.plain: It suggests other prompts, and the admin picks next steps.

example.input: A Fabrikam admin asks which sites are overshared and how risky they are.
example.output: The agent gathers the data, explains the risk levels, and suggests next steps for the admin to choose.

whenToUse: You want fast answers about content risk.
You want guided steps instead of manual reports.
whenNot: It needs SharePoint Advanced Management and a specific admin role.
It guides remediation, so admins still decide what to do.

learn.title: What is the SharePoint Admin Agent?
